Oudewater
ow'de-vah-ter
n. (small town of Holland on the Hollandse Yssel; stormed and its people killed by the Spanish army in August 1575)
Dutch Oudewater, the old water, from oud, old, and water; the town stands on the Hollandse Yssel west of Utrecht.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Oudewater is a very small town of Holland on the Hollandse Yssel, and in August 1575 it was stormed by the Spanish army under Hierges after a short siege and the greater part of its inhabitants were killed or carried off; the town was burned. It was the last of the massacres of the Dutch war and it was done on the same principle as Naarden three years earlier, with the same purpose and the same result, which is to say none. By 1575 the towns of Holland had already discovered at Haarlem, Alkmaar and Leiden what a Spanish promise was worth and what a flooded polder could do to an army, and the destruction of a town of a few thousand people altered nothing. The dictionary enters Oudewater partly to complete the record and partly for one further reason. It is the smallest and least known of these places, its name is not in the national mythology beside Alkmaar and Leiden, and almost everybody in it died; which is a reasonably good description of the circumstances of most of the people the church has ever lost, and an argument for keeping registers that do not only record the famous.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to storm as to assault a fortified place; obscure as unnoticed, not known to fame; and a register as a book of record preserved as evidence.

expand to see more

STORM, v.t. To assault; to attack and attempt to take by scaling walls, forcing gates or breaches.

OBSCURE, adj. [L. obscurus.] Not noticed; unknown to fame; unnoticed; humble; mean; not easily understood.

REGISTER, n. A written account of acts or proceedings preserved as authentic evidence; a book of record.

POLDER, n. In the Netherlands, a tract of low land reclaimed from the water and protected by dykes.

DESTRUCTION, n. [L. destructio.] The act of destroying; demolition; ruin; the state of being destroyed.

Modern Corruption

The smallest and least remembered of the Dutch war's massacred towns, stormed and destroyed in August 1575 to no military purpose.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the same policy of terror, and by 1575 it had the added character of futility: it had been tried three times and had three times produced the opposite of its aim, and it was tried again. The dictionary notes that this is the usual career of such policies. They are not abandoned when they fail, because the men who adopt them have no other method and cannot admit that the method is the problem.

The principle to recover is the keeping of the obscure. “To hear the groaning of the prisoner; to loose those that are appointed to death” (Psa 102:20) is said of God hearing people whose names no chronicle holds. “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant” (Isa 1:9) is the right frame for a town where almost everyone died. The dictionary holds that a church's register of its own losses should be kept by place and by name, and that the places which have no part in a national story are exactly the ones that will otherwise be lost.
